title: We Made This 1 Cedar Fence Picket Into a Trellis for Our Raspberry Bush | Quiet Backyard Living
description: The real QBL cedar fan-trellis build: materials, photo steps, finished pair and the later berry-patch installation.
bodyClass: rs-edition hp-edition co-edition hy-edition article-page story-edition

copy.span_2: Making & learning / One picket. A useful little idea.
copy.p_2: This is how ours came together: five strips, three spreaders, a fan shape and a few rough edges. A build story—not an exact blueprint.
copy.figcaption_1: Our finished fan trellis, before the next chapter outside.
copy.figcaption_2: Actual pieces and tools from the QBL build.
copy.span_8: The idea / Support for a raspberry bush
copy.li_1: One cedar fence picket, ripped into five ⅞-inch fan strips.
copy.li_2: The roughly ½-inch leftover strip, cut into 1-, 2- and 3-foot spreaders.
copy.li_3: Glue, pin nails and a couple of screws for the base.
copy.li_4: A garden fence post for the installed support.
copy.p_3: The source uses a table saw, pin nailer and drill. It does not document picket thickness, hardware specifications, blade setup or a complete cutting-safety method. Use appropriate tool instructions; this is the record of our build.
copy.span_9: The build / In the order it happened
copy.em_3: One small step at a time.
copy.p_4: We measured up about 10 inches, then glued and pin-nailed the five fan strips together. The source also describes glue over the lower base area. That is what we tried, not a tested claim of rot protection.
copy.h3_2: Give it a little more hold.
copy.p_5: A couple of drilled holes and screws strengthened the base before opening the fan. We learned not to run the joined section too high, or the fan would not open well.
copy.h3_3: Open the fan from the top.
copy.p_6: We centered the 3-foot spreader by eye, then glued and pin-nailed the five fan pieces into place. Balanced enough mattered more than perfect.
copy.p_7: The 2-foot and 1-foot spreaders followed. We kept them clear of the strengthened base so the shape could open naturally.
copy.p_8: A garden fence post made the installed trellis feel more solid. This is our attachment approach; the source does not establish wind or load capacity.
copy.figcaption_3: The raspberry idea became a second trellis for the blackberry bush.
copy.span_15: The result / Not staged to perfection
copy.p_9: The first little build made us happy enough to make another. The raspberries weren’t asking for perfect measurements. We wanted a useful shape and something to grow against.
copy.p_10: What we’d carry forward: leave the base short enough to open the fan, keep the spreaders away from that joined section, and plan how the finished piece will stand outside.
copy.figcaption_4: Late May 2026 · the actual fan trellis in the berry patch.
copy.span_16: What happened next / Out of the workshop
copy.p_11: The late-May journal follows the cedar trellises into the raspberry and blackberry patch. That is the next chapter we can show—not a promised harvest or a long-term durability result.
